Patient-reported symptoms:

  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Layla Al-Fayed was forty-six when she walked into the community health clinic, her leather work tote heavy with inventory sheets and a half-empty cup of cold coffee. Six years earlier, the morning had begun like any other until her seven-year-old son collapsed in their driveway, his breathing reduced to thin, desperate whistles. She called emergency services, spent the transit to the county hospital gripping the back of an ambulance seat, and watched as clinicians performed a rigid physical examination: the cool stethoscope against his collarbone, the firm pressure of a pulse oximeter on his tiny finger, the synchronized rush of needles. He had survived, but the memory of that exam and the flashing lights remained fixed in her mind. When she tried to look away from it, she found herself instead turning her mind toward the hospital corridor, wondering why the event had been allowed to unfold, questioning what she had done or failed to do, replaying the timeline in search of a pattern that would make the terror comprehensible. In the years that followed, Layla built a quiet, disciplined routine around avoiding the very objects and places that had defined that morning. She could not watch television news that featured medical emergencies, and she deliberately rerouted her commute to bypass the county hospital, taking the long arterial roads even when traffic backed up. The sound of a siren, even from blocks away, made her shoulders hike to her ears. When a patient in her pharmacy brought in a rescue inhaler, she stepped behind the counter, focused on the barcode scanner, and refused to let her fingers touch the medication until the transaction was logged. At work, where she spent her days counting tablets and verifying dosages, she held to the belief that her inability to protect her son revealed a profound weakness, and she was certain that nothing good could happen to her anymore. She viewed her fractured state as a fundamental flaw, convinced there was something wrong with her as a person. Her days unfolded under a constant, low-grade vigilance that refused to lift even when she sat alone in her sunlit apartment. She would pace the length of her kitchen, listening to the refrigerator hum, certain that her body was still braced for an emergency that had already passed. Ordinary noises—the pharmacy door chime, a neighbor’s dog barking, a dropped prescription bottle in the back room—made her jump, her breath catching in a way that felt entirely uncontrolled. Sleep offered little refuge; she lay awake for hours, her mind refusing to quiet, waking at three in the morning with her chest tight, staring at the ceiling until dawn bleached the room gray. When the quiet hours arrived, she worked hard to push any memory forward, humming classical music, or mentally reciting medication classifications until her vision blurred. The cumulative weight of these habits finally exceeded her capacity to manage them alone. She stopped accepting routine appointments for her own checkups, declining the physical examinations because the pressure of a clinician’s hands felt like a threat. Her pharmacist colleagues noticed how she withdrew during shifts that required pediatric consultations, how she systematically avoided the respiratory aisle, and how her demeanor grew increasingly distant. Her fear was not of the memories themselves, but of the conviction that her condition was permanent. She sought help not because she believed the past could be undone, but because she hoped, however faintly, to find a way to live in a present that no longer felt like a waiting room for another disaster.
